name: Cumulus
formation: Their name comes from the latin word cumulo meaning heap. Cumulus clouds form because of atmospheric convection. Air warmed by the ground begins to rise. As it does so the temperature of the air will start to drop. If the rising hot air reaches a certain level then relative humidity reaches saturation and water vapor is created resulting in a cumulus cloud.
appearance: White, fluffy clouds with flat bases and rounded tops, often isolated. Common in fair weather, though can grow larger. Bright in sunlight, darker underneath as they develop, often described as puffy or pillowy.
warningMessage: Cumulus clouds are all capable of developing into more serious storm clouds.

name: Cumulonimbus
formation: With enough atmospheric instability, moisture, and lift strong updrafts can develop in cumulus clouds leading to thunderstorm and heavy rain-producing formations
appearance: Towering, dark-bottomed clouds with flat anvil-shaped tops. Extremely tall and dense. Bring thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail, lightning, and sometimes tornadoes. Often appear ahead of cold fronts or in summer heat. They usually develop from cumulus clouds.
warningMessage: Cumulus clouds are all capable of developing into more serious storm clouds.

name: Stratus
formation: Latin prefix strato-, meaning layer. Warm moist air rises and depressurizes and settles lower to the ground according to ideal temperatures
appearance: Flat, uniform gray cloud layer that blankets the sky developing horizontally, often touching the ground as fog. Usually brings light drizzle or mist; lacks distinct features or breaks.
facts: Can accompany Crepuscular rays which happen most frequently with Stratus clouds.

name: Nimbostratus
formation: Warm, moist air slowly rises over a broad area
appearance: Thick, dark gray clouds covering the sky completely. No distinct shape or features. Bring steady, prolonged rain or snow, often over large areas, with little variation in appearance.

name: Altostratus
formation: Large-scale lifting of moist air, often preceding a warm front
appearance: Gray or blue-gray sheets covering the whole sky, with a dim sun or moon visible. Typically linked to widespread, steady precipitation in the form of rain or snow.
notes: Often a signal of incoming steady rain or snow
facts: Thicker than cirrostratus, lacks distinct features

name: Altocumulus
formation: Convection and turbulence in the mid-troposphere
appearance: White or gray patches, rolls or rounded clouds, often in layers or groups. May look like a field of cotton balls. Can precede thunderstorms when seen in humid morning skies.

weather.precipitation: Usually fair, but can precede thunderstorms

notes: Often confused with cirrocumulus, but elements are larger and lower
facts: Appearance in morning can indicate afternoon storms

name: Stratocumulus
formation: Latin prefix strato-, meaning layer. Stratocumulus clouds can form when a layer of stratus clouds begins to breaks up or striate. They can also be formed as cumulus clouds begin to flatten due to inversion of temperature or wind shear, and then become stratocumulus clouds
appearance: Low, lumpy gray or white clouds in groups or layers, often with gaps of blue sky. Rarely bring more than light rain or drizzle. Appear after stormy or unsettled weather.
warningMessage: Cumulus clouds are all capable of developing into more serious storm clouds.

name: Cirrus
formation: Latin meaning curl of hair or fringe. Cirrus clouds form from the ascent of dry air, making the small quantity of water vapour in the air undergo deposition into ice (to change from a gas directly into a solid). Cirrus is made up completely of ice crystals, which provides their white colour and form in a wide range of shapes and sizes.
appearance: Thin, wispy and feathery strands high in the sky, bright white in sunlight. They can appear in patches or narrow bands, and can have a silky or fibrous sheen. No precipitation below, but often signal approaching changes in weather or frontal systems within the next day.

weather.precipitation: They may predict the arrival or rainstorms.

name: Cirrostratus
formation: Gradual lifting of a wide air mass, often preceding a warm front
appearance: Milky, transparent veil covering much of the sky; often whitish and smooth. Produces halos around the sun or moon. Indicates moisture aloft and often precedes widespread rain or snow.

weather.precipitation: Often precedes precipitation; halo phenomenon around the sun/moon.

facts: Associated with optical phenomena like halos

name: Cirrocumulus
appearance: Small, white patches or puffs arranged in ripples or rows. Look like fish scales ('mackerel sky'). Rarely bring precipitation but may signal instability or approaching storms, especially when seen with other clouds.

weather.precipitation: Fair weather but can suggest storm development

notes: Rare and short-lived; no shadows cast
facts: Can be mistaken for altocumulus, but occurs higher and has smaller elements
